artiest/peter-kruder.text:
Peter Kruder was born in Vienna in 1967 and is an Austrian producer and DJ. Together with Richard Dorfmeister he forms the duo Kruder & Dorfmeister, and they founded the label G-Stone Recordings. Since the G-Stoned EP of 1994, Kruder has made a wide range of productions. The duo released DJ-Kicks: Kruder & Dorfmeister (1996) and The K&D Sessions (1998), which are regarded as groundbreaking for electronic music.

The sound that emerged from them is called downtempo. It showed that electronic music does not have to be cold and metallic, but can also sound sensual and full of soul. Both releases became bestsellers worldwide, and The K&D Sessions sold more than a million copies. The album is considered one of the most influential of the 1990s.

Apart from the duo, Kruder made solo work. His debut album Peace Orchestra appeared in 1999, with soul, hip hop, jazz and dub. He remixed Bebel Gilberto, among others, and in 2001 started the project Voom:Voom with Fauna Flash, a new reading of Detroit techno and deep house. He also produced for Marsmobil, Urbs and the album Teufelswerk by DJ Hell. In 2010 Kruder & Dorfmeister and G-Stone celebrated their sixteenth anniversary, with the compilation Sixteen F**kin Years of G-Stone Recordings and the live tour K&D Sessions Live.
artiest/peter-kruder.listen: Listen to a track from The K&D Sessions. Notice the calm beat, the warm sounds and the atmosphere that set downtempo apart from hard dance music.

artiest/peter-maffay.text:
Peter Maffay, born Peter Alexander Makkay, is a German singer and musician, born in 1949 in Brașov, Romania. His father was a Transylvanian Saxon. In 1963, when he was fourteen, the family moved to West Germany, and that same year he started his first band, The Dukes.

His first single, Du, became a big hit in Germany in 1970. The album Steppenwolf (1979) made him one of the biggest stars in the country and sold 1.6 million copies. The following year Revanche (1980) sold more than two million. It contains his version of Über sieben Brücken musst du gehn, a song by the East German rock band Karat from 1978. Maffay asked Karat for permission and made a new arrangement with a saxophone solo. Because Karat could not appear on West German television, his version became the well-known one in the West; it reached number four in the German chart. In this way the song became known on both sides of the Wall, and it is now regarded as one of the best-known German songs of recent decades.

Maffay also created Tabaluga, fairy tales about a little green dragon that grew into albums, a musical and tours. He holds the German record for the most number 1 albums: sixteen. He is also committed to traumatised and abused children, among other things with a farm on Mallorca where they can holiday free of charge. In 1996 he received the Bundesverdienstkreuz.
artiest/peter-maffay.listen: In Peter Maffay's version of Über sieben Brücken musst du gehn, listen to the saxophone solo he added to the arrangement. Then compare it with Karat's original recording: what changes in the mood of the song?

artiest/peter-phillips.text:
Peter Phillips is a British choral conductor, musicologist and writer. He was born in Southampton in 1953 and studied organ and music at St John's College, Oxford. There he laid the foundations of the ensemble with which his name is associated: The Tallis Scholars. The first concert took place on 3 November 1973 in a church in Oxford. The choir consisted of singers from the great Oxbridge chapels and from the start chose an individual repertoire that explored forgotten corners of English and continental polyphony.

In 1980 Phillips founded the record label Gimell. With it he filled gaps in the catalogue with seldom-recorded composers such as Cardoso, White, Gombert and Fayrfax. In 1987 a recording by the Tallis Scholars won the Gramophone Record of the Year award. That was the start of a project that lasted until 2021: all the masses of Josquin des Prez on disc, in honour of the five-hundredth anniversary of the composer's death. The discography also includes masses by Palestrina, requiems by Victoria and works by Byrd and Tallis, often with a pure, clear sound that lets every voice be heard.

Phillips also worked with living composers, above all John Tavener, whom he met in 1977. Later Eric Whitacre, Nico Muhly and David Lang, among others, were added. His choir gave most of its concerts outside the United Kingdom and introduced a large audience to Renaissance polyphony.
artiest/peter-phillips.listen: Listen to Spem in alium by Thomas Tallis as performed by the Tallis Scholars and try to hear how the voices move through the space like waves. Notice how clear every singer remains, even as the sound builds.

artiest/peter-pringle.text:
Peter Pringle is a Canadian musician and television personality, born in 1945. At the age of six he was already singing in the children's choir of the Canadian Opera Company. Later he studied several classical instruments, including lute, sitar and surbahar, and paid for his studies by writing pop songs. Anne Murray recorded some of those songs, and he also sang backing vocals for her.

In 1975 he moved to Los Angeles, where his first album appeared in 1976. In 1980 he went to Montreal and recorded pop songs in English and French. He was twice nominated for a Juno Award as most promising male vocalist, in 1978 and 1982. In 1985 he took part in the French-language charity single Les Yeux de la faim for the famine in Ethiopia. In 1986 he received a Genie Award nomination for the song Cold As Ice, which he wrote with Kevin Hunter for the film Toby McTeague. He also presented television shows and, from 1987, performed a one-man show about Noël Coward. The album Noel Coward: A Portrait came out of it.

Since 2007 he has attracted attention online with ancient epics and poems, which he performs on his YouTube channel. He plays a wide variety of instruments, from the lyre to the hurdy-gurdy, and delivers many of the texts in their original ancient languages. His recording of the opening lines of the Epic of Gilgamesh has been viewed more than thirteen million times. In this way he is an example of a musician who brings ancient music and texts to a new audience through the internet. In the course he appears with The Silver Lyre of Ur from 2025.
artiest/peter-pringle.listen: Listen to The Silver Lyre of Ur. Notice the timbre of the lyre and how you can hear an ancient instrument with a soft, clear tone.

artiest/peter-schilling.text:
Peter Schilling, really Pierre Michael Schilling, is a German synth-pop singer and composer, born in Stuttgart in 1956. He is counted among the Neue Deutsche Welle, the wave of German-language new wave and pop around 1980. His songs are often about science fiction: aliens, astronauts and disasters.

His breakthrough was Major Tom (völlig losgelöst) in 1982, which reached number 1 in Germany, Switzerland and Austria. The song builds on Space Oddity (1969) by David Bowie, about the astronaut Major Tom floating through space, cut off from the earth. The album Fehler im System followed. The English-language version, Error in the System (1983), produced his only international hit: Major Tom (Coming Home), which reached number 1 in Canada and number 14 in the United States. In 1983 Die Wüste lebt also reached the top 10 in Germany, and in 1984 the album 120 Grad followed.

In 1990 Schilling suffered burnout and took a break. In his book Völlig losgelöst (2013) he describes how he came back from it. Since the 2000s he has been touring again with a band through Germany, Switzerland and Austria, and since 2018 he has voiced Major Tom in a radio play series for children. His old songs have received new attention since 2020, partly thanks to his YouTube channel. Major Tom shows how a German artist took up a British pop story and wrote a sequel to it in his own language.
artiest/peter-schilling.listen: In Major Tom (völlig losgelöst), listen to the synthesizers and the tight electronic beat, typical of the Neue Deutsche Welle. Then compare the story with Space Oddity by David Bowie: what happens to Major Tom in each song?

artiest/peter-tosh.text:
Peter Tosh was born Winston Hubert McIntosh in Westmoreland, Jamaica, in 1944. His parents abandoned him and he grew up with relatives. As a teenager he moved to Kingston. He taught himself guitar by watching another player for hours. At the lessons of the singing teacher Joe Higgs, who taught young people for free, he met Bob Marley and Bunny Wailer. From 1962 they sang together on the street corners of Trenchtown.

In 1964 they formed the Wailing Wailers, later The Wailers, and scored a big ska hit with Simmer Down. At the beginning Tosh was the only one who could play instruments, and the others learned from him. Together they became Rastafarians and slowed their music down, first to rocksteady and then to reggae, with political and social lyrics. Tosh co-wrote Get Up, Stand Up. After Catch a Fire and Burnin' (1973), he and Bunny Wailer left the group, dissatisfied with label boss Chris Blackwell.

As a solo artist Tosh was the most militant of the three. His debut Legalize It (1976) became an anthem for the legalisation of cannabis, and Equal Rights (1977) demanded equal rights and justice. He sang against apartheid and often became a target of the Jamaican police for it. On the Rolling Stones' own label he sang a duet with Mick Jagger. In 1983 Mama Africa appeared, containing his reggae version of Johnny B. Goode. Tosh was murdered in a robbery at his home in 1987.
artiest/peter-tosh.listen: Listen to Johnny B. Goode by Peter Tosh and compare it with the rock 'n' roll of Chuck Berry. Notice how the guitar now plays on the offbeat and how the tempo becomes slower and heavier.

artiest/peter-zinovieff.text:
Peter Zinovieff (1933 to 2021) was a British composer, musician and inventor. He was born into a Russian noble family that had fled to England before the revolution, and took a doctorate in geology at Oxford. His real love was electronic music. With the proceeds of an auctioned tiara he bought a computer, which he connected, at his house in Putney, to oscillators and amplifiers from army surplus. By his own account it was the first computer in a private home anywhere in the world.

In 1966 and 1967, with Delia Derbyshire and Brian Hodgson, he ran the organisation Unit Delta Plus, which aimed to make and promote electronic music. His system MUSYS grew into the company Electronic Music Studios, EMS for short. In 1968 his Partita for Unattended Computer received its premiere in London: the first performance of live computer music without a human performer, read from paper tape.

His company made the VCS3, a compact synthesizer that was cheaper and more portable than the large Moog system. Early progressive rock bands such as Pink Floyd and White Noise used it, as did Krautrock groups and pop musicians such as Todd Rundgren and David Bowie. Zinovieff himself had little interest in pop music and later worked mainly as a composer of electronic music. His importance lies in the equipment: he gave a whole generation of rock musicians access to sounds that had previously been heard only in experimental music studios.
artiest/peter-zinovieff.listen: Listen to a track from the 1970s on which the VCS3 can be heard, such as an early Pink Floyd, and notice the whooshing, almost alien sounds that no guitar or keyboard would make. Try to hear what is electronic and what is not.

artiest/pharoah-sanders.text: Ferrell 'Pharoah' Sanders, from Little Rock, came to New York in 1962, where he lived on the street for a while. Sun Ra gave him his stage name. From 1965 he played in the group of John Coltrane, his great example, and he stayed until Coltrane's death. Sanders could make his tenor saxophone scream with overtones and overblowing, but he also played tenderly and melodically. Karma (1969) contains The Creator Has a Master Plan, well over half an hour long, with the singer Leon Thomas. He became the most important voice of spiritual jazz. In 2021, at the age of eighty, he recorded Promises with the British producer Floating Points and the London Symphony Orchestra.
artiest/pharoah-sanders.listen: Hear how the saxophone alternates between a calm melody and eruptions of overtones.

artiest/pharrell-williams.text:
Pharrell Williams is an American singer, songwriter, producer and fashion designer, born in Virginia Beach in 1973. At a summer camp for school orchestras he met Chad Hugo. Williams played drums, Hugo tenor saxophone. In 1992 they started the production duo The Neptunes together. In 1999 they formed the band N.E.R.D. with Shay Haley, in which Williams sang. Together they also founded the label Star Trak Entertainment in 2001.

As a producer, Williams delivered many hits in hip hop and R&B in the years around 2000. As a solo artist he broke through with Frontin' in 2003, followed by the album In My Mind in 2006. In 2013 he was behind two worldwide hits: Blurred Lines by Robin Thicke and Get Lucky by Daft Punk, on which Nile Rodgers also plays. That same year Happy appeared, written for the film Despicable Me 2. It was the run-up to his album Girl in 2014. He has won thirteen Grammys, including three times as producer of the year, and has been nominated twice for an Oscar.

Williams is regarded as one of the most influential producers of modern pop music. His sound is stripped-down and rhythmic, with a sharp ear for a striking drum pattern and a groove you recognise immediately. Since 2023 he has also been creative director of menswear at Louis Vuitton.
artiest/pharrell-williams.listen: Listen to Happy and notice how little is actually needed: a solid beat, handclaps and a light singing voice together create the mood. Try to hear which element carries the song.

artiest/phife-dawg.text:
Phife Dawg's real name was Malik Izaak Taylor, and he was born in Queens, New York, in 1970 to Trinidadian parents. His mother was a poet. He had known Q-Tip since the age of two. When he was nine he heard Rapper's Delight by the Sugarhill Gang and suggested rapping together. In 1985 they formed the group Quest, later A Tribe Called Quest, with DJ Ali Shaheed Muhammad, and Jarobi White joined as well. Because of his height of 1.60 metres, Phife was nicknamed the Five-Foot Assassin.

A Tribe Called Quest belonged to the collective Native Tongues, together with De La Soul and the Jungle Brothers. The debut People's Instinctive Travels and the Paths of Rhythm appeared in 1990 on Jive Records. On The Low End Theory of 1991 Phife took on a bigger role and also rapped about social issues. Midnight Marauders followed in 1993, Beats, Rhymes and Life in 1996 and The Love Movement in 1998. Tensions with the label and within the group led to the end.

Phife also worked with others and released his solo debut Ventilation: Da LP in 2000. In 2015 he and Q-Tip decided to put their quarrel aside and secretly make a new album. Phife died in March 2016. We Got It from Here... Thank You 4 Your Service was completed without him. His sharp, playful voice alongside Q-Tip's calmer flow gave the group its characteristic interplay.
artiest/phife-dawg.listen: Listen to a track by A Tribe Called Quest and notice the interplay between two voices. Try to hear how Phife, with his rawer, faster voice, contrasts with Q-Tip.

artiest/phil-cohran.text:
Phil Cohran (1927 to 2017) was an American jazz musician, born in Oxford, Mississippi, and raised in Missouri. In the early 1950s he played trumpet in the band of Jay McShann and then in a US Navy band. In 1959 the saxophonist John Gilmore brought him to the Sun Ra Arkestra in Chicago. Cohran played with them until 1961, mostly trumpet and sometimes a stringed instrument such as the zither, and can be heard on albums such as Fate In A Pleasant Mood and Angels and Demons at Play. When the orchestra left Chicago, he stayed behind.

In 1965 he helped found the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians (AACM). He formed the Artistic Heritage Ensemble, with which he recorded the album On the Beach around 1967. In that year he also started the Afro-Arts Theater, a centre for African American musicians on the South Side of Chicago. By then he played harp, cornet, horn, baritone saxophone and percussion.

Cohran also devised an instrument of his own, the Frankiphone or Space Harp: an electrically amplified mbira or kalimba. The instrument featured on early Sun Ra records and inspired Maurice White to use an electric kalimba with Earth, Wind and Fire. According to Cohran, he taught White and his brothers in their youth. Eight of the nine members of the Hypnotic Brass Ensemble are his sons. He taught young people and adults in Chicago well into old age.
artiest/phil-cohran.listen: Listen to the title track of On the Beach and try to hear the Frankiphone, the electric thumb piano. Notice how soft and metallic it sounds compared with trumpet or drums.

artiest/phil-collins.text:
Phil Collins is an English drummer, singer and songwriter, born in West London in 1951. He began drumming at the age of five and worked as a child actor, playing the Artful Dodger in the West End production of Oliver!, among other roles. In 1970 he became the drummer of Genesis. When Peter Gabriel left in 1975, Collins took over the vocals, and under his leadership the group moved from progressive rock towards more accessible pop and rock. In addition, he played in the jazz fusion group Brand X from 1975 to 1979.

His solo career began in 1981 with Face Value, an album shaped by his first failed marriage and his love of soul. Hello, I Must Be Going! followed in 1982, No Jacket Required in 1985 and ...But Seriously in 1989. Well-known singles include In the Air Tonight, Against All Odds (Take a Look at Me Now), Sussudio and Another Day in Paradise. He won an Oscar for the music of Tarzan from 1999. In 1996 he left Genesis, and in 2010 he was inducted with the group into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Collins is known for the gated reverb, a drum sound with a short, powerful reverb effect that could be heard everywhere in pop and rock in the 1980s. Rolling Stone ranks him among the hundred best drummers of all time. His work with Genesis, his solo records and his collaborations gave him more American top 40 hits in the 1980s than any other artist.
artiest/phil-collins.listen: Listen to In the Air Tonight and notice the moment when the drums come in. Try to hear how big and hard the drum sound is, above all because of the reverb effect.

artiest/phil-everly.text:
Phil Everly (1939 to 2014) was the younger half of The Everly Brothers, the duo he formed with his brother Don. He was born in Chicago, the son of the guitarist Ike Everly. In 1953 the family moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, and the brothers later went to Nashville. Their career as a duo had already begun in 1951. In 1957 they signed with Cadence Records and had their first hit with Bye Bye Love, written by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant. The song had been turned down by thirty other artists and became their first million-seller.

Cathy's Clown and All I Have to Do Is Dream are also among their big hits. Phil wrote When Will I Be Loved himself and worked with Don on songs such as The Price of Love. After quarrels the duo split up, and both brothers went solo from 1973 to 1983. In 1983 they came together again on the stage of the Royal Albert Hall in London. The album EB '84, produced by Dave Edmunds, followed. In 1986 they were the first duo to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

The hallmark of the Everlys was the close harmony singing of two brothers, which had a great influence on later pop groups, above all through its harmony. Paul McCartney said that when he and John Lennon wrote their first songs, they imitated the Everlys: he played Phil, Lennon played Don.
artiest/phil-everly.listen: Listen to All I Have to Do Is Dream and notice the two voices singing so close together that they almost sound like one. Try to hear where they part.

artiest/phil-medley.text:
Phil Medley (1916 to 1997) was an American songwriter. He is best known as the writer of Twist and Shout, which he composed with Bert Russell, also known as Bert Berns. The song became world famous through the performances of the Isley Brothers and The Beatles. In all, more than sixty covers of Twist and Shout have appeared. Medley died in New York in 1997, aged 81.

He wrote alone and with others, including Russell, William Stanford, Victor Abrams and Bob Elgin. With Russell he wrote If I Didn't Have a Dime, which was released by Gene Pitney in 1962. It was also the first song that the Dutch band The Cats put out as a single. He wrote A Million to One and was co-author of Killer Joe, which was recorded by the Rocky Fellers, The Rivieras and The Kingsmen, among others. In 1962 he composed and produced the song Limbo Lucy for Capitol Records for the group The Everglades, whose manager he was.

Medley belongs to the generation of songwriters who hardly appeared in the picture themselves, but whose songs were made big by others. His most important song is a dance number with a short, rousing build-up that lent itself easily to covers in widely differing styles. His compositions are still being reissued in the twenty-first century.
artiest/phil-medley.listen: Compare Twist and Shout by the Isley Brothers with the version by The Beatles. Notice how the vocals become louder and rawer as the song goes on.

artiest/phil-oakey.text:
Philip Oakey is an English singer and songwriter, born in Hinckley in 1955 and raised in Sheffield, among other places. He is the frontman and co-founder of the synth-pop group The Human League. His musical career began by chance in 1977. He had bought a saxophone but gave up learning it, and had no plans to join a band. His old schoolmate Martyn Ware was looking for a singer for the group The Future, in which Ware and Ian Craig Marsh used analogue synthesizers instead of ordinary instruments. Ware left a note on Oakey's front door. Oakey knew little about music, but was known in Sheffield for his unconventional clothes.

In 1977 the group was renamed The Human League. The first performance was in 1978, after which they signed with Fast Records. In 1981 the breakthrough came with The Sound of the Crowd, Love Action (I Believe In Love) and the album Dare. Oakey co-wrote and sang Don't You Want Me, a song that reached number one in the United States and in Britain. In the early 1980s he stood out with an unusual haircut: long on one side, short on the other.

Outside the group Oakey worked with the producer Giorgio Moroder. Their song Together in Electric Dreams, for the 1984 film Electric Dreams, became an international hit. A year later the album Philip Oakey & Giorgio Moroder followed. As the singer of The Human League he has been at the front for more than forty years in a style that definitively linked pop music with synthesizers.
artiest/phil-oakey.listen: Listen to Don't You Want Me and notice the alternation between Oakey's low, almost monotone voice and the lighter vocal part that answers it. Hear, too, how the synthesizers carry the rhythm.

artiest/phil-spector.text:
Phil Spector was born in the Bronx, New York, in 1939. He was an American producer who showed in the early 1960s that the producer could be the real creator of a record. With him the singers were almost interchangeable: He's a Rebel was released under the name The Crystals, but was sung by Darlene Love and The Blossoms.

In 1958, as a member of The Teddy Bears, he had already had a number 1 in America with To Know Him Is to Love Him. In 1961 he started the record label Philles with Lester Sill. At Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles he worked with a regular group of studio musicians, later known as The Wrecking Crew. They played the same parts simultaneously on several pianos and guitars, with a lot of reverb. That became the Wall of Sound. Examples are He's a Rebel by The Crystals (1962), Be My Baby by The Ronettes (1963) and You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' by The Righteous Brothers (1964). River Deep – Mountain High by Ike & Tina Turner (1966) reached only number 88 in America, but number 3 in England.

Spector later produced Let It Be (1970) by The Beatles, and worked on Imagine by John Lennon and All Things Must Pass by George Harrison. Bruce Springsteen modelled Born to Run (1975) on the Wall of Sound, and in Stockholm ABBA borrowed the doubling of instruments. In 2003 Spector shot the actress Lana Clarkson dead in his home. In 2009 he was convicted of her murder.
artiest/phil-spector.listen: Be My Baby by The Ronettes (1963) begins with only the drum pattern of Hal Blaine. Then listen to how, layer by layer, pianos, guitars, strings and percussion come in and merge into one wall of reverb.

artiest/phil-wilde.text:
Phil Wilde, really Filip De Wilde, is a Belgian producer and DJ, born in Antwerp in 1967. He began in the 1980s as a DJ at the TOP studio in Ghent and made his first recordings under names such as Uniform and, with Patrick De Meyer, T99. In 1989 he produced Laat je gaan by Petra & Co, which reached number 1 and went gold.

In Antwerp he met Jean-Paul De Coster. Together they made the single Don't Miss the Party Line under the name Bizz Nizz, which reached the top 10 in England. In May 1991 they built the instrumental Get Ready for This in their studio, to which they wanted to add rap. The Dutch rapper Ray Slijngaard added vocals and also brought in the singer Anita Doth: this is how 2 Unlimited came into being. In Belgium the group signed with Byte Records, which licensed the records to labels in other countries, such as PWL Continental in England. In 1993 No Limit became a worldwide hit. Wilde and De Coster devised and built the music; Ray and Anita gave the project a face.

After 2 Unlimited, Wilde carried on producing and remixing, for Kate Ryan, among others, whose Désenchantée was number 1 in Belgium, and even for Kabouter Plop. In 2009 he helped the original singers of 2 Unlimited with the music for their reunion shows. His career shows how Eurodance worked in the 1990s: the producers stayed in the background while others stood on stage.
artiest/phil-wilde.listen: In Get Ready for This, listen to the hard, fast synthesizer riff that opens the track and keeps coming back. Notice how little singing there is: the track revolves around the beat and the riff, with only short shouts and a few lines of rap.

artiest/philadelphia-orchestra.text:
The Philadelphia Orchestra is an American symphony orchestra from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and belongs to the Big Five of American orchestras. It was founded in 1900 by Fritz Scheel, who was also its first conductor. In 1904 Richard Strauss conducted the orchestra in a programme of his own works, and in 1906 the Polish pianist Arthur Rubinstein made his American debut with it. Until 2001 the orchestra played in the Academy of Music, afterwards in the Kimmel Center, where the hall is now called Marian Anderson Hall. In summer it plays at the Mann Center.

The orchestra rose to national fame under Leopold Stokowski, who became music director in 1912. In 1936 Eugene Ormandy joined him, and from 1938 to 1980 Ormandy was the sole music director. Riccardo Muti, Wolfgang Sawallisch, Christoph Eschenbach and, since 2012, Yannick Nézet-Séguin followed. From the beginning the orchestra recorded a great deal, mainly for RCA Victor and Columbia. Sergei Rachmaninoff himself conducted it in his own works in 1929. In 2011 it became the first major American orchestra to file for bankruptcy; the proceedings were concluded in 2012.

The Philadelphia Orchestra is known for its long series of recordings and for its rich, full string sound. It is regarded as one of the defining American orchestras of the twentieth century.
artiest/philadelphia-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording of the orchestra under Ormandy or Stokowski and notice the warm, full sound of the strings. Try to hear how that section plays as a single instrument.

artiest/philharmonia-orchestra.text:
The Philharmonia Orchestra is a British orchestra from London, founded in 1945 by Walter Legge, a record producer at EMI. Legge had already used the name in 1941 for a string quartet. He put the orchestra together from young musicians who were still in the armed forces and above all wanted to make good recordings. At first it did not exist as a permanent ensemble, but was called up each time from players on Legge's list. The first concert in 1946 was conducted by Thomas Beecham, but the orchestra did not want him as its permanent conductor. In its early days it worked with Richard Strauss, Wilhelm Furtwängler and Arturo Toscanini, and Herbert von Karajan became closely associated with it.

From the late 1950s to the early 1970s Otto Klemperer was principal conductor. In 1964 Legge wanted to disband the orchestra, but the musicians carried on as a self-governing ensemble under the name New Philharmonia Orchestra. After thirteen years they regained the original name. Riccardo Muti revitalised the orchestra from 1972 to 1982. Giuseppe Sinopoli, Christoph von Dohnányi, Esa-Pekka Salonen and, from 2021, Santtu-Matias Rouvali followed.

The orchestra gives more than a hundred and sixty concerts a year, tours widely and has commissioned more than a hundred new compositions. In its first twenty years it was regarded as the best symphony orchestra in London.
artiest/philharmonia-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording of the Philharmonia Orchestra under Klemperer and notice the authority and calm with which the orchestra plays. Try to hear how the winds and strings keep each other in balance.

artiest/philharmonia-orchestra-en-willia.text:
William Walton was an English composer who wrote the music for fourteen films between 1934 and 1969. He was helped by Hyam Greenbaum and later by Roy Douglas, who orchestrated short pieces under his supervision. Walton did not like film music being performed in the concert hall. In his view, film music was not good film music if you could use it for anything else. Even so, he made a few exceptions, above all for the music to Henry V, Hamlet and Richard III.

The film Henry V, based on Shakespeare's play, appeared in November 1944. Walton wrote the music in 1943 and 1944, and the London Symphony Orchestra recorded it under the direction of Muir Mathieson. Two separate movements, for strings alone, were allowed to be heard in the concert hall: the passacaglia The Death of Falstaff and Touch Her Soft Lips and Part. Walton conducted them himself with the Philharmonia Orchestra for a record that appeared in 1946 on HMV. That London orchestra also played the music for the film Hamlet of 1948. Later Malcolm Sargent, Muir Mathieson and Christopher Palmer made suites of it, and in 1963 Walton himself conducted the recording of Mathieson's suite.

A passacaglia is a form in which a short bass or theme motif keeps returning. That suits a deathbed: the piece sounds measured and solemn. The examples of Henry V, Hamlet and Richard III show that film music could also live on outside the cinema. For the history of pop this is important because Walton's film music forms a tradition from which later film composers drew.
artiest/philharmonia-orchestra-en-willia.listen: Listen to Henry V Suite: Passacaglia, The Death of Falstaff. Notice the strings alone: how does the music sound measured and sad, and how does the melody keep returning?

artiest/philip-glass.text: Philip Glass was born in Baltimore in 1937, studied in Chicago and at Juilliard and then in Paris with Nadia Boulanger. There he also worked with the Indian sitar player Ravi Shankar. From this grew his minimalist style: short figures that repeat endlessly and change slowly, often in broken chords. In Godfrey Reggio's Koyaanisqatsi (1982), a film without dialogue, image and music together carry the story. For Paul Schrader's Mishima (1985) he wrote for string quartet and orchestra. For Martin Scorsese he made Kundun (1997). He contributed a few pieces to The Truman Show (1998), and The Hours (2002) earned him an Oscar nomination. His pulsing patterns have been heard everywhere in film music ever since.
artiest/philip-glass.listen: Pay attention to the repetition: hear how a short pattern returns dozens of times and how each time one note, chord or instrument changes.

artiest/philip-glass-ensemble.text:
The Philip Glass Ensemble is an American group, founded in 1968 by the composer Philip Glass as a vehicle for performing his experimental, minimalist music. The ensemble still exists and is under the musical direction of the keyboard player Michael Riesman. The line-up became a hallmark of Glass's early style: amplified woodwinds, usually saxophones, flutes and bass clarinet, electronic keyboards and a solo soprano singing solfège, that is, the syllables of the note names instead of a text.

In 1976 Glass wrote his first opera, Einstein on the Beach, for the ensemble. After that he wrote more often for other line-ups, but the core remained. In 2011 the ensemble played a series of concerts in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, at the Temple of Dendur. Between 2012 and 2015 it performed Einstein on the Beach again, starting in Montpellier. In 2013 it began again with La Belle et la Bête, an opera to accompany the 1946 film by Jean Cocteau. In 2014 Glass appeared on stage with Steve Reich for the first time in more than thirty years, at the Next Wave Festival in Brooklyn. In 2018 the ensemble played Music With Changing Parts at Carnegie Hall, a work said to have changed the music of the 1970s, with the San Francisco Girls Chorus.

The importance of the group is that Glass could determine and perform his own instrumental sound. The repeating patterns and the unceasing rhythm brought minimal music to a wide audience, far beyond the classical concert hall.
artiest/philip-glass-ensemble.listen: Listen to a piece by Philip Glass played by his own ensemble and follow one repeating motif in the keyboards or the woodwinds. Notice how small shifts make the whole sound different every time.

artiest/philip-jones-brass-ensemble.text:
The Philip Jones Brass Ensemble was founded in 1951 by the trumpeter Philip Jones and was one of the first modern classical brass ensembles. The group played as a quintet, or as a ten-piece ensemble for larger halls. It toured and recorded a great deal, and numerous arrangements were commissioned for it. After Jones's death a large part of them went to the library of the Royal Northern College of Music in Manchester.

The line-up consisted of trumpets, horns, trombones, tuba and percussion, sometimes with a conductor such as Elgar Howarth or John Iveson. The ensemble recorded Leonard Salzedo's signature fanfare for the Open University television broadcasts. When Jones stopped in 1986, many members continued to work together under the name London Brass.

The group showed that brass can do more than military music or a single fanfare. With chamber music for brass players, arrangements of older and newer music and a sound that was both full and precise, the ensemble gave the genre a permanent place in the concert hall. In doing so it set an example for later brass quintets.
artiest/philip-jones-brass-ensemble.listen: Listen to a recording of the Philip Jones Brass Ensemble and try to keep the individual brass voices apart. Notice how the trumpets carry the melody and the trombones and tuba lay the foundation.

artiest/philip-koutev.text:
Philip Koutev, in Bulgarian Filip Kutev, was a Bulgarian composer and arranger, born in 1903 in Aytos and died in 1982. In 1951, with his wife Maria Kuteva, he founded the State Ensemble for Folk Song and Dance, the first professional, state-funded ensemble in Bulgaria. That ensemble also bears his name and is called the Filip Kutev Ensemble.

Koutev developed a way of arranging folk songs. He combined elements of folk music with forms and harmonies from Western classical music. In this way he created a new Bulgarian choral tradition. His choir was one of the four heard on the album Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares, Volume Two. That album won a Grammy Award in 1989 and brought Bulgarian choral music to an audience in the rest of the world.

In this way Koutev stands at the origin of the sound that many listeners outside Bulgaria associate with the music of that country. His work shows how a composer can bring tradition and modern arrangement together. A mountain in Antarctica, Kutev Peak, is named after him.
artiest/philip-koutev.listen: Listen to a track from Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares and notice the sharp, open choral sound. Try to hear where the melody is carried by a single voice and where the other voices set harmonies against it.

artiest/philip-koutev-ensemble.text:
Filip Kutev, often spelled Philip Koutev in the Western manner, was a Bulgarian composer and arranger, born in 1903 in Aytos. In 1951, together with his wife Maria Kuteva, he founded Bulgaria's first professional, state-funded ensemble: the State Ensemble for Folk Song and Dance, also known as the Filip Kutev Ensemble. His name has remained attached to the choir to this day.

With this ensemble Kutev paved the way for a new way of arranging folk songs. He combined elements of folk music with Western classical forms and harmonies. In this way a new Bulgarian choral tradition came into being, which gave a stage to a people with a rich singing culture. The records show it, for example Koutev Bulgarian National Ensemble (1963) and Bulgarian Polyphony, which appeared in 1989 and 1990. The word polyphony means a great deal in Bulgarian, because the choirs sing in tense, sharp harmonies.

The choir was one of the four choirs on the album Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares, Volume Two, which won a Grammy in 1989. That brought Bulgarian singing to a worldwide audience, far beyond the country's borders. Kutev died in 1982. A mountain peak in Antarctica bears his name. The course chooses Polegnala e Todora from 1998, a folk song that is heard in such choral arrangements.
artiest/philip-koutev-ensemble.listen: Listen to Polegnala e Todora. Notice the women's voices singing together and the sharp, tense harmonies they form.

artiest/philippe-de-vitry.text:
Philippe de Vitry (1291 to 1361) was a French composer, poet, bishop and music theorist of the late Middle Ages. Little is known about his youth. He probably studied in Paris, because in documents he is called magister. Later he worked at the courts of Charles IV, Philip VI and John II as secretary and adviser, was a canon in several places and served for a time in the retinue of the pope in Avignon. He was also a diplomat and a soldier. In 1351 he became bishop of Meaux. He knew the Italian scholar Petrarch, who praised him as a keen seeker after truth, and the mathematician and music theorist Nicole Oresme.

In music history he is best known for the treatise Ars nova notandi of 1322, which gave its name to the music of his time, the ars nova. His authorship, and even the existence of the text as we know it, has been called into question. Little of his composition has survived, and only his sacred works have come down to us, even though he also wrote secular music. His motets from the Roman de Fauvel are attributed to his style.

Vitry's importance lies in notation, above all rhythm and the division of the beat. These innovations made possible the free and complex music of the following century. In this way he determined how polyphonic music was set down on paper from the fourteenth century onwards.
artiest/philippe-de-vitry.listen: Listen to a motet from the Roman de Fauvel and notice how the upper voices and the low voice each have a rhythm of their own. Try to hear that the voices move almost independently of one another.

artiest/philippe-herreweghe.text:
Philippe Herreweghe is a Belgian conductor and choral conductor, born in Ghent in 1947. He received piano lessons from his mother and at university combined studies in medicine and psychiatry with musical training at the Ghent Conservatory. In 1970 he founded the Collegium Vocale Gent with fellow students. Nikolaus Harnoncourt and Gustav Leonhardt heard his approach and invited him and his choir to take part in their recordings of all the Bach cantatas.

In 1977 Herreweghe started the ensemble La Chapelle Royale in Paris for French music of the golden age, with Lully, Charpentier and Campra, among others. From 1982 to 2002 he was artistic director of the Académies Musicales de Saintes. He also started the Ensemble Vocal Européen, specialising in Renaissance polyphony, and in 1991 the Orchestre des Champs Élysées, which plays Classical and Romantic music on original instruments. Since 1997 he has been principal conductor of the Antwerp Symphony Orchestra, and he also conducts renowned guest orchestras, such as the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra.

He is best known for his Bach interpretations. His repertoire runs from the Renaissance to the early Romantic period, with excursions into Beethoven and Mahler. He aims for a historically informed and well-considered performance. In this way he belongs to the conductors who brought early music back to life with small forces and often on authentic instruments.
artiest/philippe-herreweghe.listen: Listen to a Bach cantata under Herreweghe and notice the balance between the small choir and the orchestra. Try to hear how clear every voice remains, even in the busy passages.

artiest/philippe-verdelot.text:
Philippe Verdelot was a French Renaissance composer who spent most of his life in Italy. He was born between 1480 and 1485 in Les Loges, in the French region of Seine-et-Marne, and died between 1530 and 1540. Little is known about his early life. He probably came to Italy young and worked in cities in the north, possibly also in Venice. From 1523 to 1525 he was maestro di cappella at the baptistery of Florence, and until 1527 possibly also at the cathedral.

In 1526 he collaborated on the staging of La Mandragola, the cynical comedy by Niccolò Machiavelli. The songs he wrote for it, called canzone, are regarded as the earliest madrigals. For that reason he is often called the father of the Italian madrigal, and he was one of the first and most prolific composers of the genre. His motets also reveal his political sympathies: he probably supported the reformer Girolamo Savonarola, as appears from his setting of In te domine speravi and from his motet Letamini in domino.

Verdelot possibly died during the siege of Florence in 1529 and 1530, or from the plague that was then raging in the city. After 1530 there is no evidence that he was still alive. His madrigals set an example for later Italian composers and taught them to keep the music close to the meaning of a poem.
artiest/philippe-verdelot.listen: Listen to a madrigal by Verdelot and notice how the voices alternate and also sing together. Try to hear whether the music follows the words of the text.

artiest/philly-joe-jones.text:
Philly Joe Jones (1923 to 1985) was an American jazz drummer. His nickname referred to his home town of Philadelphia and avoided confusion with the older drummer Papa Jo Jones. As a child he performed as a tap dancer on a radio programme. In 1947 he became house drummer at Café Society in New York, where he played with the most important bebop musicians of his time, including Tadd Dameron.

His best-known period fell between 1955 and 1958, when he toured and recorded with the Miles Davis Quintet, with Red Garland on piano, John Coltrane on saxophone and Paul Chambers on bass. Davis called him his favourite drummer and wrote in his autobiography that he always went on listening to him in other drummers. Bill Evans, too, openly called him his favourite. From 1958 Jones worked as a bandleader and as an accompanist to Evans and Hank Mobley, among others.

Between 1967 and 1972 he lived in London and Paris, where he played with Archie Shepp and Mal Waldron. He recorded the album Mo' Joe in London in 1968. In 1981 he founded the group Dameronia, devoted to the music of Tadd Dameron, and led it until his death. He was known for being able to adapt his playing to any group and any soloist. This made him one of the most sought-after drummers of modern jazz.
artiest/philly-joe-jones.listen: Listen to a track by the Miles Davis Quintet from the years 1955 to 1958 and notice the drumming behind the soloist. Try to hear how the drummer pushes the soloist on with accents on the snare drum.

artiest/phoenix.text:
Phoenix is a French rock band from Versailles, formed in 1995. The line-up has never changed: Thomas Mars sings and plays drums, Deck d'Arcy plays bass and keyboards, and Christian Mazzalai and Laurent Brancowitz play guitar. Mars, d'Arcy and Mazzalai knew each other from school and at first rehearsed as a garage band at Mars's home. Brancowitz joined after his earlier band Darlin' had stopped. That band also included Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, who later formed Daft Punk. In 1997 they chose the name Phoenix, pressed 500 copies of a first single on their own label Ghettoblaster and signed with Source Records in Paris.

The breakthrough came in 2009 with the fourth album Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix, with the singles 1901 and Lisztomania. It won a Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album. In 2013 Bankrupt! appeared, with which the band headlined Coachella and Primavera Sound. Ti Amo from 2017 is influenced by Italo disco, and Alpha Zulu from 2022 was recorded in the Louvre, in memory of the producer Philippe Zdar. In 2024 the band played at the closing ceremony of the Olympic Games in Paris.

The music is described as indie pop, synth-pop, pop rock and new wave. Phoenix shows that French pop music could succeed internationally in English, with a clear and melodic sound that combines guitars and synthesizers.
artiest/phoenix.listen: Listen to 1901 and notice how the guitars and the synthesizers together form one tight, sunny pattern. Try to hear which part carries the melody and which the rhythm.

artiest/phuture.text:
Phuture is a house group from Chicago, founded in 1985 by Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr., Nathaniel Pierre Jones, better known as DJ Pierre, and Herbert 'Herb J' Jackson. With a single record, Acid Tracks (1987), the group gave a new style a sound and a name: acid house.

The heart of Acid Tracks is the Roland TB-303, a small bass machine that Roland made from 1981 to 1984 to imitate a bass guitar. Phuture had the 303 repeat a short bass line and turned the knobs of the filter while it played. In this way the same line constantly changes its sound: squealing, squelching and wailing. Underneath run Roland's TR-707 and TR-727 drum machines. The group began work on the track at the end of 1985, when it was first called In Your Mind. DJ Ron Hardy played a tape of it at the Music Box, the club where he was resident DJ. The first time the dance floor emptied, but Hardy kept playing it again that evening, and the crowd came round. Fans called it Ron Hardy's Acid Track, and that is how the title came about. In 1987 the track, of more than twelve minutes, was released on the Chicago label Trax Records, with Marshall Jefferson as producer.

Acid Tracks is often cited as the first acid house track. In 1988 acid house became a mass youth culture in England, with clubs such as Shoom in London and the Haçienda in Manchester and the first raves. In 2022 Rolling Stone placed the track at number 118 in a list of the 200 greatest dance songs of all time. DJ Pierre later continued the group.
artiest/phuture.listen: In Acid Tracks, listen to the TB-303 bass line: the notes stay the same, but by turning the filter open and closed the sound changes constantly, from a dull hum to a sharp, squelching squeal. Notice, too, how long it lasts: the track was made to keep running in a club, not as a pop single.

artiest/pierre-barouh.text:
Pierre Barouh (1934 to 2016) was a French writer, composer and singer, born in Paris as Élie Pierre Barouh. His parents were Turkish-Jewish market traders. During the war they hid their children from the Nazis in the French countryside, a period that later inspired songs such as La Bicyclette, Des ronds dans l'eau and Les Filles du dimanche. After the war he was briefly a sports journalist and played in the B team of the French volleyball squad. In Portugal he came to know Brazilian music, and in 1959 he travelled to Brazil. Back in Paris he became friends with Brazilian writers and composers of bossa nova.

With his first earnings he bought a mill in the Vendée, where he set up a recording studio. In 1965 he started the label Saravah, with which he wanted to mix musicians and styles. He worked there with Brigitte Fontaine, Jacques Higelin, Nana Vasconcelos and Elis Regina, among others. As a singer he had success with La Plage, made known by Marie Laforêt and the guitarist Claude Ciari, and with Tes dix-huit ans and Monsieur de Furstenberg.

His best-known work is the film Un homme et une femme by Claude Lelouch from 1966, which won the Palme d'Or at Cannes. Barouh played a part in it and sang the words to the music of Francis Lai. That year he also married the actress Anouk Aimée; three years later they separated. He also made a documentary about the early years of bossa nova. In this way he brought Brazilian influences to French chanson.
artiest/pierre-barouh.listen: Listen to the title song of Un homme et une femme and notice how the singing and the scat syllables together create an almost danceable, relaxed mood. Try to hear where the bossa nova groove comes through.

artiest/pierre-boulez.text: Pierre Boulez studied with Messiaen in Paris and after the war became the sharpest spokesman of the avant-garde. He extended Webern's serial technique to duration, dynamics and timbre. His Le marteau sans maître of 1955, on poems by René Char, sets an alto voice beside alto flute, viola, guitar, vibraphone and percussion, in a light, sparkling sound. Later he founded the research institute IRCAM and became a celebrated conductor.
artiest/pierre-boulez.listen: Listen to the beginning of Le marteau sans maître and hear how alto flute, guitar, vibraphone and percussion exchange short, glittering fragments without a fixed pulse.

artiest/pierre-henry.text:
Pierre Henry (1927 to 2017) was a French composer, best known for his contribution to musique concrète, music made from recorded sounds. He was born in Paris and at the age of fifteen was already experimenting with the sounds of all kinds of objects. From 1938 to 1948 he studied at the Conservatoire de Paris, with Nadia Boulanger and Olivier Messiaen, among others. Between 1949 and 1958 he worked at the Club d'Essai studio of French radio, founded by Pierre Schaeffer. With Schaeffer he wrote Symphonie pour un homme seul in 1950, an important early example of the genre.

Henry wrote the first musique concrète in a commercial film, Astrologie ou le miroir de la vie from 1952, and made much more film and ballet music. Two years after he left the radio, he founded Studio Apsone-Cabasse with Jean Baronnet, the first private studio for electronic music in France. In 1967, with Michel Colombier and the choreographer Maurice Béjart, he made the ballet Messe pour le temps présent. In 1970 he recorded the album Ceremony with the British rock band Spooky Tooth.

His influence extends to pop music. Psyché Rock from 1967 inspired Christopher Tyng in the theme of the animated series Futurama. The sounds from Jericho Jerk became a favourite sample in hip hop and electronic music, with D'Angelo, A Tribe Called Quest and James Blake, among others. In 1997 artists such as Fatboy Slim and Coldcut made remixes of his work.
artiest/pierre-henry.listen: Listen to Psyché Rock and notice the repeating bass motif with the fast, electronic sounds around it. Then compare it with the theme of Futurama.

artiest/pierre-michelot.text:
Pierre Michelot (1928 to 2005) was a French jazz bassist and arranger, born in Saint-Denis near Paris. He learned piano from 1936 to 1938 and at sixteen switched to double bass. After the war he played for American soldiers in France, and in the 1950s he was often asked for by American musicians performing in Paris. In 1948 he played with Rex Stewart, in 1949 with Kenny Clarke at Frisco's in Paris, and in the winter of 1949 to 1950 with Coleman Hawkins, with whom he also recorded. That year he also played with Clarke in a group led by Sidney Bechet.

In the course of his career Michelot also worked with Django Reinhardt, Stéphane Grappelli, Thelonious Monk, Lester Young, Dexter Gordon, Stan Getz, Bud Powell, Dizzy Gillespie and Chet Baker. In 1957 he worked with Miles Davis on the music for Louis Malle's film Ascenseur pour l'échafaud. He was a member of the Jacques Loussier Trio, which became known from 1959 with the Play Bach series, jazz arrangements of music by Johann Sebastian Bach. From the early 1960s to about twenty years later he concentrated mainly on arranging and studio work.

In 1986 he appeared in Bertrand Tavernier's film Round Midnight, a part he owed to Dexter Gordon, the film's lead, with whom he had made records in 1963. Michelot was a bassist who felt at home among European and American musicians. He died in Paris in 2005 of Alzheimer's disease.
artiest/pierre-michelot.listen: Listen to the music of Ascenseur pour l'échafaud and notice Miles Davis's trumpet in the quiet, sombre atmosphere. Try to hear how the rhythm section, in which Michelot plays bass, carries that atmosphere.

artiest/pierre-schaeffer.text:
Pierre Schaeffer was a French composer, writer, radio maker and engineer. He was born in Nancy in 1910. His father was a violinist and his mother a singer, but his parents steered him towards engineering. He studied at the École Polytechnique in Paris and first worked as a telecommunications engineer in Strasbourg. From 1936 he worked for French radio in Paris. In 1942 he founded the Studio d'Essai there, which played a part in the Resistance during the war and afterwards became a centre for new music.

At the radio Schaeffer was allowed to experiment with records and equipment. He played sounds backwards, slowed them down and sped them up and layered them over one another. Those techniques were then almost unknown. His first complete work based on those experiments was Étude aux chemins de fer (1948), made from recordings of trains. This is how musique concrète came into being: music that does not begin with notes on paper, but with recorded sounds from reality. From 1949 he worked with Pierre Henry, including on Symphonie pour un homme seul (1950). In 1951 he set up a research group with a studio containing a tape recorder. He is regarded as the first composer to make music with magnetic tape.

Schaeffer died in 1995. His techniques later became commonplace in every studio: sampling, cutting and pasting and sound manipulation have since been the basis of much pop music. Jean-Michel Jarre was also one of his students.
artiest/pierre-schaeffer.listen: Listen to Étude aux chemins de fer and try to recognise the sounds of trains: wheels, steam, whistles. Notice how Schaeffer repeats those sounds and turns them into a rhythm.

artiest/piet-souer.text:
Piet Souer is a Dutch producer, songwriter and arranger, born in 1948. He began as a guitarist and keyboard player with The Valiants, a rock band from Eindhoven. His breakthrough came when he played guitar on De troubadour by Lenny Kuhr, the winner of the 1969 Eurovision Song Contest. A year later, with Kuhr and the bassist Paul Reekers, he was the support act for Georges Brassens on his tour of France.

In the early 1970s he wrote and arranged hits such as Te veel te vaak by Liesbeth List and Samen by Liesbeth List and Ramses Shaffy. After that he produced for Champagne, Mouth & MacNeal, Anita Meyer and American Gypsy, among others, and worked with international artists such as Vicky Leandros and Engelbert Humperdinck. In 1976, with the producer Hans van Hemert and the manager Han Meijer, he formed the girl trio Luv'. Souer and Van Hemert wrote the songs under the pseudonyms Janschen and Janschens, including You're the Greatest Lover, Trojan Horse and Casanova. In 1982 Tight Fit reached the top five in Britain with his song Fantasy Island.

Souer wrote two Eurovision songs, Sing Me a Song in 1983 and De eerste keer in 1996, which both finished seventh. He also composed a great deal of film music and television jingles, including for Suske en Wiske, Spoorloos and the Dutch version of Lingo. He received twenty-two gold and platinum records. His work shows how much Dutch pop music of the 1970s and 1980s came out of the studio.
artiest/piet-souer.listen: Listen to You're the Greatest Lover by Luv' and notice the danceable, tight accompaniment and the layered vocals of the trio. Try to hear what is singing and what is studio work.
